claims.claim: Communication is the transfer of information and meaning between people: CFI defines communication as transferring information to produce greater understanding, and the Saylor textbook defines it as the process of understanding and sharing meaning; the lesson's working definition is attributed to these two sources.

A communication episode can be broken into named parts — sender, message, channel, receiver, feedback, and noise — and the Saylor textbook lists source, message, channel, receiver, feedback, environment, context, and interference as its eight essential components.

In OpenStax's basic communication model, the communicator (sender) encodes a message — translating ideas into a systematic set of symbols (language), written or spoken — and the receiver decodes it, attaching meaning influenced by the receiver's own experiences and frame of reference.

Feedback is the receiver's response that completes a communication episode; OpenStax notes it may take forms such as a verbal response, a nod of the head, a request for more information, or no response at all.

Noise is anything that blocks or changes the intended meaning of a message: OpenStax describes noise as factors that distort message clarity at any point in the model, including the decoding process, and the Saylor textbook calls it interference, including psychological noise when a person's own thoughts occupy their attention.

Communication can be verbal (spoken or written words) or nonverbal (meaning carried without words): OpenStax names oral and written communication among the types that occur in organizations and describes nonverbal communication as the transformation of information without speaking or writing — body language, facial expression, and even office size and placement; CFI lists vocal, written, visual, and non-verbal means, including body language, gestures, pitch of voice, and tone.

Organizations have formal and informal communication routes: formal channels follow the official structure (OpenStax describes interpersonal communication as reinforcing the formal structure of the organization by making use of formal channels), while the grapevine is the informal network — OpenStax describes managers gathering information from the grapevine and passing along viewpoints that have not yet reached the more formal channels, and notes a web of informal personal connections exists beyond the organization chart.

Clear communication practice means knowing the audience, saying it plainly, and checking understanding: the Saylor textbook ties clarity to choosing words and phrases the audience understands and avoiding jargon or slang that may be unfamiliar, and CFI emphasizes active listening, conciseness, and using the correct medium (serious matters such as layoffs or salary changes discussed in person, not by email).

The honest framing — meaning is what the receiver takes away — follows from OpenStax's account of decoding (the receiver attaches meaning to the message, shaped by the receiver's experiences and frame of reference) and from the Saylor textbook's receiver component (the receiver analyzes and interprets the message in ways both intended and unintended by the source).

conflictingEvidence.issue: How many parts the message model has
positions: The Saylor textbook names eight essential components: source, message, channel, receiver, feedback, environment, context, and interference.
OpenStax 16.1 presents a simpler episode: a communicator encodes a message, a receiver decodes it, with feedback and noise as additional elements.

This lesson uses a six-part simplification — sender, message, channel, receiver, feedback, noise — that keeps the spine common to both treatments, folding environment and context into the situation rather than giving them separate slots.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The six-part model is presented as a teaching simplification, not as a competing theory; it is consistent with both source treatments, and the sources are cited for the parts they explicitly name.

CFI and the Saylor textbook are also used reference-only; no source prose is reproduced in the lesson.

sourceRecords.title: Communication: A Vital Life Skill
sourceRecords.notes: Tier B. Read live via HTTP on 2026-08-22. Supports: communication defined as transferring information to produce greater understanding; communication done vocally, through written media, visually, or non-verbally (body language, gestures, pitch of voice, and tone); from a business standpoint all transactions result from communication; a 2016 LinkedIn survey ranking communication the most sought-after soft skill among U.S. employers; improving communication through active listening, conciseness, body language, and using the correct medium (serious matters such as layoffs or salary changes discussed in person, not by email); signs of poor communication (wrong medium, failing to listen). Facts restated in original prose; all lesson examples are original.

sourceRecords.title: Business Communication for Success
sourceRecords.provider: Saylor Foundation (open textbook; University of Minnesota Libraries edition)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier B OER. Downloaded the PDF and read chapter 1 on 2026-08-22. Supports: communication defined as the process of understanding and sharing meaning (the Latin root communicare means to share or make common); the eight essential components (source, message, channel, receiver, feedback, environment, context, interference); the source encoding the message and watching the audience's reaction; the message as the stimulus or meaning produced by the source for the receiver; the channel as the way a message travels between source and receiver (spoken channels like face-to-face conversation and telephone, written channels like letters, email, and texts); the receiver analyzing and interpreting the message in ways both intended and unintended; interference, also called noise, as anything that blocks or changes the source's intended meaning, including psychological noise; clarity as choosing words the audience understands and avoiding jargon or slang; context playing a very important role in communication, particularly across cultures.

sourceRecords.title: Principles of Management, Section 16.1: The Process of Managerial Communication
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A (open textbook). openstax.org blocks direct fetching; verified via Wayback Machine capture web.archive.org/web/20200815141803/ of the canonical section URL on 2026-08-22. Supports: the basic communication model in which a communicator encodes a message and a receiver decodes it; encoding as translating ideas into a systematic set of symbols (language), written or spoken, influenced by the sender's experience, emotional state, and the people involved; decoding as the recipient interpreting the message and attaching meaning, influenced by the receiver's experiences and frame of reference; feedback as the last step in completing a communication episode (a verbal response, a nod, a request for more information, or no response; informational, corrective, and reinforcing types); noise as factors that distort message clarity at any point in the model, including the decoding process; interpersonal communication as the vehicle for providing, receiving, and exchanging information that reinforces the formal structure of the organization through formal channels. Facts restated in original prose; the book's footer states it may not be used to train or be ingested into LLMs without permission, so usage is REFERENCE_ONLY.

sourceRecords.title: Principles of Management, Section 16.2: Types of Communications in Organizations
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A (open textbook). Verified via Wayback Machine capture web.archive.org/web/20200926094106/ of the canonical section URL on 2026-08-22. Supports: oral communication (spoken, the most prevalent type) and written communication (email, texts, letters, reports, manuals; preferred for important messages such as a change in company policy, where precision and documentation matter); nonverbal communication as the transformation of information without speaking or writing — body language, facial expression, and signals such as office size and placement; major influences on interpersonal communication: social influences (status barriers, prevailing norms and roles), perception (how the receiver perceives the sender shapes reception), interaction involvement (attentiveness), and organizational design (messages passing through multiple levels can be distorted); the informal organization as a web of informal personal connections between workers that exists beyond the organization chart. Facts restated in original prose (REFERENCE_ONLY).

sourceRecords.title: Principles of Management, Section 16.5: The Major Channels of Management Communication Are Talking, Listening, Reading, and Writing
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A (open textbook). Verified via Wayback Machine capture web.archive.org/web/20200920205427/ of the canonical section URL on 2026-08-22. Supports: the major channels of managerial communication as talking, listening, reading, and writing, with talking the predominant method and managers spending about 75% of their time in verbal interaction (Borden); one-on-one conversations in informal venues as a main route for exchanging, validating, and confirming information; the grapevine — shrewd managers gather information informally from the grapevine, listen in on office gossip, and pass along viewpoints that have not yet made their way to the more formal channels of communication; writing's role in documenting the most important projects, decisions, and ideas. Facts restated in original prose (REFERENCE_ONLY).
